claims.text: Service-relevant thermal exposure causes diffusion-controlled nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds in the metastable Mg-containing alloy.
The intermetallic compounds are expected to involve elements such as Mg, Ti, and Zn.
Fine, uniformly distributed intermetallics help produce a stable Ti/Mg-rich protective oxide.
A stable Ti/Mg-rich protective oxide retains corrosion resistance.
A stable Ti/Mg-rich protective oxide retains high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Rapid intermetallic coarsening and clustering locally deplete key alloying elements.
Local alloying-element depletion impairs formation of a coherent passivating film and degrades environmental resistance.
Nonequilibrium processing can produce a refined, metastable microstructure containing phases far from equilibrium.
The initial alloy is a single-phase solid solution with minimal intermetallic content.
Isothermal annealing transforms the metastable solid solution into a dual-phase microstructure containing intermetallic precipitates.
Intermetallic phases nucleate, grow, and coarsen both at grain boundaries and within grain interiors.
Intermetallic development changes local composition and the nature of the surface oxide layer.
During annealing, alloying elements partition from the supersaturated solid solution into intermetallic compounds.
Coarse intermetallics create galvanic sites that reduce corrosion resistance.
Mg-Ti-Zn-based multicomponent alloy design can provide favorable corrosion potential and low corrosion current density relative to common Mg alloys.
Annealing will produce new intermetallic phases relative to the as-processed baseline.
Corrosion current density will correlate with intermetallic volume fraction, size, and distribution.
Oxide-film integrity and thickness will correlate with intermetallic volume fraction, size, and distribution.
Mechanical alloying can extend the solid solubility of Ti and Zn in Mg and can improve corrosion resistance.
